paragraphs.text: Walking home late one night this week, I paused to register the perfect quiet, the air sweet with the scent of decaying leaves: the city in October, when the cold is still just flirting. The simple delight that Emily Brontë observed — “Every leaf speaks bliss to me / Fluttering from the autumn tree” — seemed attainable. What a waste to go inside and go to sleep when being out in the fresh night feels this good.

Fall is a season that rewards outdoorsy people, those who have been waiting patiently for the heat to break and the mosquitoes to retreat so they can layer on their wicking fabrics and take to the trails. The word “outdoorsy” is one that bedevils me: It’s one of those noun-turned-adjectives that purports to simply describe a person who likes to be in nature, but implies virtue. An outdoorsy person is healthy, active, connected to the earth. An indoorsy person, by contrast, is sedentary, vitamin D-deficient, screen-addicted. I aspire to all the moral characteristics of the outdoorsy set, and so have spent my adult life trying to become a person who can follow color-coded trail markers through the spruces.

Outdoor Boys, a YouTube channel with over 20 million subscribers, features people going to the furthest extremes of outdoorsiness: camping on frozen oceans, building survival shelters in blizzards, catching and cooking snakes. Natalie Berry, a freelancer, wrote about the phenomenon in The Times this week. The videos are “usually enjoyed indoors, by a predominantly male audience, who find comfort in watching others overcome discomfort,” she noted. They’re like housecats watching pumas and jaguars stalk jungle prey from the comfort of their living-room sun puddles.

Getting comfortable with discomfort seems to me to be the key to living a bigger, more fulfilling life. A few years ago, I had the rather rudimentary realization that my aversion to being cold was causing me to shrink my life to fit within the walls of my apartment during winter. I’d decline invitations, measuring the worthiness of an activity by its proximity to a thermostat. When I realized being cold is not an emergency — it’s just discomfort, and discomfort can be tolerated — I got a better winter coat and stopped dreading February so much.

Outdoorsiness as an identity, however, has continued to elude me. There’s a certain amount of skill that goes into erecting a tent, rappelling down a rock face. On message boards where people ask how they can become more outdoorsy, the advice is to start slow: Go to a park and build an evening campfire before planning a weeklong camping trip. Those of us who aspire to outdoorsy might embrace the alternate descriptor outsidey in the meantime. “Outdoorsy is nature for adventure. Outsidey is nature for leisure,” goes a TikTok on the distinction. Mountaineering is for the outdoorsy, it explains, whereas an outsidey person will “frolic upon the meadow.” It’s a lighthearted differentiation, but the ultimate effect is one of inclusiveness. You don’t have to summit a mountain in order to appreciate the foliage. You don’t have to be athletic or intrepid in order to be connected to the natural world.
THE LATEST NEWS
• President Trump said he directed the Justice Department to block certification of the Alaska Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses by a narrow margin.

• The Justice Department filed a lawsuit yesterday arguing that the results could be tainted by voter confusion over the fact that there is challenger on the ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whose name is so similar to the incumbent’s, Dan S. Sullivan.
• And these are just two of the steps raising fears that Trump is laying the groundwork to challenge the results of the election if he doesn’t like the outcome.
More on Politics

• Senators from both parties have told the White House that they will block all Trump nominees from getting confirmed until the administration restores satellite communications capabilities used by Ukraine’s military.
• The Justice Department accused two former F.B.I. officials of lying to Congress about investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of the former president.
• Here’s what Democrats plan to do with their power if they win back Congress
Around the World

• Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three others in the occupied West Bank on Friday. Israeli forces shot dead the assailants, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu promised a major operation on the neighborhood of Hebron where they are from.
• Melania Trump, the first lady, said that she had brokered a local cease-fire between Russian and Ukrainian forces in a southern Ukrainian city.
• France has deployed 70,000 police officers today in hopes of avoiding a repeat of last weekend’s unrest.
• “I have to go in”: The father credited with stopping the gunman who killed three students and a teacher at an Oregon elementary school gave his first public account of how it happened.
• New data shows a drop in the number of ninth-grade girls who identify as bisexual. Researchers are debating what it means.
• Read our review of the new foldable iPhone.
THE INTERVIEW
— Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor of Texas. Click here to watch, listen or read her conversation with Lulu Garcia-Navarro.
GAME OF THE WEEK

Green Bay Packers vs. Detroit Lions: It’s a good time to be a football fan in the Midwest. N.F.L. teams in Chicago, Kansas City, Green Bay, Detroit, Minnesota, Cincinnati and Cleveland all have winning records as we approach Week 7, and the region’s N.F.C. North is the only division in which every team has better than 50 percent odds to make the playoffs. Tomorrow at 4:25 p.m. Eastern, two longtime rivals from that division face off in Detroit’s climate-controlled dome. The Packers are riding on momentum after three straight wins. The Lions have benefited from the steady hand of their quarterback, Jared Goff. —Matthew Cullen
Plus: Here’s what they are talking about on all of those N.F.L. headsets.
THE WEEK IN CULTURE
Film and TV
• Elizabeth Holmes let the makers of “You Can See Everything” dissect her lies. On our “Hard Fork” podcast, three reporters who have covered Holmes dissect why no one can look away.
• In “A Talent for Murder,” Helen Mirren plays the reclusive and curmudgeonly novelist Patricia Highsmith — except she’s a suspicious character in a thriller. Is it believable?
• The music world for years sneered at Billy Corgan, the frontman of the Smashing Pumpkins. Now, as young fans rediscover his music, he’s sneering back. Listen to his interview on Popcast.
• Twenty years after Amy Winehouse released “Back to Black,” her fans still can’t get enough.
• A Claude Monet painting of flowers in his Giverny water garden sold for about $56 million. Why do wealthy collectors covet his work?
• Art Basel announced that the Paris edition of the fair was ending early for safety reasons, as the city braces for another weekend of protests.
RECIPE OF THE WEEK
Roasted Red Pepper and Feta Cornbread

There are so many ways to bake a batch of cornbread. Sweet or savory, firm or fluffy, plain or loaded with aromatics and cheese: You really can’t go wrong. Lidey Heuck adds roasted red pepper and feta to her easy cornbread recipe, giving the loaf pockets of tangy cheesiness. The sour cream in the batter means this won’t dry out if you want to make it a day ahead — that is, if you can resist a pan of warm cornbread cooling on your counter. I can’t.
REAL ESTATE
The Hunt: A family with deep Chicago roots left Illinois for a job in New York with $1.8 million to spend on a new home. What did they find? Play our game.
What you get for $1 million: A Colonial Revival in Janesville, Wis., a Second Empire house in Rollinsford, N.H., and a bungalow in Nashville are all on the market. Which would you choose?
Settling down: Gig economy workers face higher scrutiny in getting a mortgage than those with traditional incomes. Here’s what to know.
LIVING
Compounding: A couple built a 10,000 square-foot residence in Palm Desert, Calif., to compel their adult children to visit. Did it work?
Meaningful minimalism: A Los Angeles couple took inspiration from Shaker design to create an office that embodies work-life balance.
High water mark: New innovations help homes in low-lying areas stay dry even as sea levels rise.
ADVICE FROM WIRECUTTER
How to find the perfect jeans

A great pair of jeans should survive every trend cycle, work with nearly everything in your closet and hold up to frequent wear. These are the things our experts considered as they tested nearly 100 pairs to find the very best men’s jeans and women’s jeans. Looking for your perfect pair? Consider what kind of shape you want. A slim-straight silhouette never goes out of style and works just as well with button-ups and blazers as with tees and sweaters. Opt for a relaxed, baggier pair if you want to feel more on-trend. You don’t you have to spend much to get something of quality. There are plenty of chic, well-made pairs for less than $50. —Erin Neil
